description: One corpus, run by every runtime that resolves a locale. PowerShell, Go and the browser each answer these, and they answer identically or one of them is wrong. Matching is what decides which catalog a reader gets, so a disagreement between runtimes shows up as a page in one language and a transcript in another.

cases.name: exact supported tag
cases.why: The ordinary case: the reader asked for something shipped.

cases.name: declared English alias retains its requested tag
cases.why: The manifest owns language-only aliases, and provenance retains what selected the regional catalog.

cases.name: POSIX English spelling is canonicalized before matching
cases.why: Headers and process/config inputs share one canonical tag boundary, including underscore-to-hyphen conversion.

cases.name: case is not significant in a tag
cases.why: BCP 47 tags are case-insensitive; a client sending pt-br means pt-BR.

cases.name: underscore is canonicalized to a hyphen
cases.why: POSIX-style pt_BR reaches this from process culture and from hand-edited config.

cases.name: declared language-only alias
cases.why: pt is not itself supported; the manifest declares which region it means.

cases.name: declared regional alias
cases.why: pt-PT is a different region, and the manifest says it maps to the one shipped catalog rather than falling to English.

cases.name: undeclared region of a supported language falls back
cases.why: pt-AO is not declared. Guessing that any pt means pt-BR is how a reader gets a dialect nobody reviewed; the safe answer is the default.

cases.name: unsupported language falls back
quality weights are honored, not document order
cases.why: The client's preference is the q value, not the order it happened to serialize.

cases.name: a higher-weighted unsupported tag does not win
q=0 is a refusal, not a weak preference
cases.why: RFC 9110: q=0 means 'not acceptable'. Treating it as 0.0-but-still-a-candidate serves a language the client explicitly rejected.

cases.name: every candidate refused falls back to the default
wildcard alone takes the default rather than the first supported tag
cases.why: * expresses no preference. Answering it with anything but the default makes the served language depend on table order.

cases.name: wildcard after a supported tag does not override it
duplicate tags keep the highest weight
malformed q rejects its candidate rather than becoming one
cases.why: A header is attacker-reachable. A bad q must not throw, and retaining the initial q=1 would promote malformed input above valid preferences.

cases.name: a valid lower-weight candidate beats a malformed q candidate
cases.why: This competitive case distinguishes rejecting the malformed candidate from silently keeping its initial q=1.

cases.name: a bare q rejects only its candidate
cases.why: Ignoring a bare q would retain the implicit maximum and defeat a valid lower-weight preference.

cases.name: repeated q parameters reject only their candidate
cases.why: A repeated weight is malformed rather than an instruction to choose whichever occurrence a runtime happens to read last.

cases.name: equal weights use resolved-tag order rather than header order
cases.why: A deterministic ordinal tie-break keeps the answer identical across map implementations and header serialization order.

cases.name: empty header
punctuation-only header
a tag longer than the limit is discarded
cases.why: maxTagLength bounds the work and keeps an absurd tag out of a cache key.

cases.name: an oversized header is discarded whole
cases.why: Bounded before parsing: a megabyte of tags is not a preference, it is a way to spend the server's time.

cases.name: a path traversal in a tag never selects an asset
cases.why: The resolved tag names a file. An unsupported tag must fall back rather than reach the filesystem.

cases.name: a tag carrying a separator is rejected
the lab-wide config lock beats the header
cases.why: language: in test.config.yml is the operator's decision for the whole lab; a browser cannot override it.

cases.name: the config lock beats process culture too
language: auto is not a lock
cases.why: auto is the shipped default in the template, and must behave as though nothing were configured.

cases.name: language: AUTO is the same unlocked sentinel
cases.why: Configuration scalars are read case-insensitively at this boundary; casing the sentinel must not turn it into an unsupported lock.

cases.name: an explicit user preference wins only while config is unlocked
cases.why: A persisted web choice is authoritative after language: auto, and is resolved once before the page is rendered.

cases.name: the config lock beats an explicit user preference
cases.why: A lab-wide operator lock cannot be overridden by one browser.

cases.name: an unsupported user preference falls through while config is unlocked
cases.why: A stale cookie for a locale no longer shipped must not suppress a valid request header.

cases.name: an unsupported config lock is refused, not obeyed
cases.why: A typo in config must not serve a catalog that does not exist; it resolves to the default and says the source was config.

cases.name: an invalid config lock cannot leak into provenance
cases.why: The config remains the source that suppressed lower-precedence inputs, but a path-shaped value is not a locale tag and must not reach HTML, logs or cache metadata.

cases.name: an overlong config lock cannot leak into provenance
cases.why: Config is operator-controlled rather than trusted; the same tag bound used for matching also bounds the context that downstream renderers embed.

cases.name: process culture is used when no header is present
cases.why: The CLI has no Accept-Language; $PSUICulture is its signal.

cases.name: a header outranks process culture when both are present
cases.why: A request is answered for whoever sent it, not for the account the service runs under.

cases.name: nothing at all resolves to the default
